**The difficulty moved from the hardware into the guidance, and the force table shows the move.** At three metres per second the modern capture is 4.59 times the vehicle's weight over ten centimetres, worse than the snatch. **The gentleness comes entirely from arriving slowly**, and arriving slowly is the guidance problem the previous sections spent their arithmetic on. The 1960 system needed a line, a winch and a brake that could absorb a hundred and sixty kilojoules without parting, and it needed almost nothing of the capsule, which was a passenger. **The 2021 system needs almost nothing of the structure and everything of the vehicle**, which must fly itself to a relative velocity near zero and hold a position to inches while it does.

**Neither problem is easier. They are different problems wearing the same photograph.**

### The Parasite Aircraft Were a Third Thing Again

The nineteen forties and fifties produced several attempts at carrying and recovering an aeroplane in flight, and none of them is the same problem either. The XF-85 Goblin was to hook onto a trapeze lowered from a B-36 \[[McDonnell XF-85 Goblin][ref_xf85]\], the Fighter Conveyor programme, abbreviated FICON, carried an RF-84K in a B-36's bomb bay \[[FICON project][ref_ficon]\], and the airships of the nineteen thirties carried aeroplanes on a trapeze and recovered them in flight \[[USS Akron][ref_akron]\].

**Every one of those was flown by a pilot who was aboard the aeroplane being recovered.** The FICON hookups were challenging for experienced test pilots in ideal conditions and difficult in combat or bad weather, several RF-84Ks were damaged attempting them, and the wingtip-towing project was cancelled when aerial refuelling promised a safer way of extending a fighter's range \[[FICON project][ref_ficon]\]. **The X-61A's contribution is not that the manoeuvre was done. It is that nobody was aboard**, and the loop that closed it, which the arithmetic above puts at about a quarter of a hertz, was autonomous \[[Dynetics][ref_prn_second_flight]\].

## What the Data Changed

**The programme moved exactly one thing from unknown to known, and it is a large thing.** The agency's release reports an airborne recovery of the vehicle to the C-130 \[[DARPA][ref_darpa_recovery]\], the contractor calls it historic \[[Leidos][ref_leidos_captured]\], and the specialist directory records it as the first time an X-61A was retrieved in mid-air, after several unsuccessful attempts \[[Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_dusrm_x61]\]. **None of the three claims a first of its kind for uncrewed aircraft in general, and this article does not either**, though nothing in a survey of 5,700 records describes an earlier one, and the third test series calling its nine attempts the programme's first ever is consistent with it. **The feasibility question is closed and the reliability question is untouched.**

Three quantitative things follow from the record.

**The tolerance is inches and that is now documented rather than inferred.** Nine attempts that each came within inches establish both that the system could get that close repeatedly and that the last few inches were a different problem from the first hundred feet.

**The refurbishment claim has one data point.** One vehicle was turned round and flown again within either twenty-four hours or twenty-four working hours, depending on which participant is describing it. **One instance of a twenty-fold reuse claim is not a demonstration of it and the article says so.**

**And the fleet attrition is measured even though it is not a measure of the design.** Two of five airframes were lost in nine sorties, one to a parachute that is not part of the operational system and one to a power fault whose cause was found and fixed. **The rate is 22.2 percent per sortie on a first-of-type development article, and quoting it as a property of the vehicle would be a mistake.** It is quoted here because the twenty-use requirement is a reliability claim and this is the only reliability data the programme produced. Setting that rate into the expected-sorties relation of the section on attrition gives the figures the next paragraph uses.

$$
\epsilon = \frac{2}{9} = 0.222 , \qquad \bar{n} = \frac{1 - \left( 7/9 \right)^{20}}{2/9} = 4.47 , \qquad \frac{\bar{n}}{N} = \frac{4.47}{20} = 0.224
$$

**The two halves of that sentence meet.** A design life saturates against attrition, so a twenty-use requirement makes sense only if the loss rate is well below five percent per sortie. **At the rate the development programme showed, a twenty-use airframe delivers 4.47 sorties**, 22.4 percent of what the requirement asks for. **Nobody claims that rate is what a mature system would show**, and this article does not either. The record does show that the requirement and the only measured rate are on opposite sides of the point where the requirement stops meaning anything.

**A fourth thing follows from the contract rather than from the flying.** The money stopped 47 days after the recovery and the period of performance ran on for another 1,463 days without it. **A programme that stops paying and stays open has decided something**, even if no document records the decision, and the previous article in this series found a programme that did the reverse.

| **Total** | **5,700** |

The survey behind this article holds **5,700 research records**, drawn from the Crossref registry and from the two agency report servers. **886 of them, 15.5 percent, are report primaries**, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. 5,484 records carry a usable year, running from 1930 to 2026 with a median of 2011. **4,446 of those, 81.1 percent, predate or share the year of the programme's last flight test series.**

**Every research record in the survey is cited below, each in the one cluster its title belongs to.** The clusters run from the capture itself outward, through the hardware and the flying around it, to the aerodynamics and the atmosphere the sizing arithmetic uses.

### Catching it, which is the whole of the problem

**The keystone.** Mid-air retrieval of payloads descending under parachutes, aerial recovery of uncrewed aircraft by a carrier, net, ship and ground capture, and launch and recovery systems for remotely piloted vehicles. **18 titles name mid-air retrieval and 8 of them predate 2000, while 22 name aerial recovery or the mothership and cable-drogue system and 21 of those date from 2009 or later**, which is the shape Comparison With Ground Prediction describes.

### The towed body it has to dock with, and the cable that holds it

**The towed body and its cable, in air and in water.** Towed-body and cable statics and dynamics, towed targets and decoys, the refuelling hose and drogue, and the vortex-induced vibration of circular cylinders, which is the crossflow motion of a cable segment. **147 titles are on vortex-induced vibration and 85 on the refuelling hose and drogue**, so the cluster is as much about a cylinder in crossflow as about a body on a string.

### The vehicle, the programme and the vehicles it is measured against

**The vehicle and its comparators.** The C-130 that carries and catches it, the Tomahawk and air-launched cruise missile family that shares its engine, the Corona capsule recoveries that came before it, and small expendable aircraft such as Coyote. **No title in the survey names the X-61A or Gremlins**, which is why the programme's own record is carried by the primary documents.

### The parachute, which is how it comes down when it is not caught

**Coming down when it is not caught.** Parachute and decelerator design, inflation, opening loads, stability and materials, and parachute recovery of uncrewed aircraft, boosters and capsules. **57 titles name Orion, Mars, Viking or a supersonic decelerator test programme and 11 name an uncrewed aircraft or a drone**, so the parachute literature is mostly a spacecraft literature.

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**The framing of this article is that the capture is the programme and the vehicle is not, and there are three places where that is too tidy.**

**The vehicle is not free.** Treating the airframe as a solved cruise missile ignores that it had to fold into a C-130's cargo compartment, deploy its wings after release, start a cold engine at altitude, and survive a parachute landing \[[Kratos][ref_kratos_first_flight]\] \[[Leidos][ref_leidos_captured]\]. **The width of 0.57 metres against a span of 3.47 is a folding requirement and it constrains the wing that the recovery requires to be large** \[[Dynetics X-61 Gremlins][ref_x61_wikipedia]\].

$$
b_p = \frac{b_v - w}{2}
$$

Each panel is 1.45 metres, 0.345 of the body it must lie along, and the deployed span is 6.09 body widths. **Those two requirements pull opposite ways and the article has not priced the conflict**, because the chord is not published and the panel's stowed thickness is not either.

**The economics rest on a number nobody measured.** Every statement above about cost per sortie takes the twenty-use life as given, and the programme demonstrated 9 percent of it. **If the practical life were five rather than twenty the architecture still pays on the arithmetic here, so the conclusion is robust, but the specific figures are not.**

**And the C-130 is treated as free, which it is not.** A recovery sortie costs a transport aircraft, its crew and its fuel, and that cost is divided by however many vehicles come home on it. **The programme demonstrated one.** At one vehicle per sortie the recovery aircraft's share is the dominant term in the cost identity and this article cannot evaluate it, because no participant has published what a recovery sortie costs.

**One further thing is absent rather than wrong.** The article has said nothing about what the vehicles were for. The payloads named in the public descriptions are electro-optical sensors, infrared imagers, electronic warfare systems and weapons \[[Dynetics X-61 Gremlins][ref_x61_wikipedia]\], and the operational concept is a volley launched from outside the defended area \[[DARPA][ref_darpa_gremlins]\]. **The volley concept is the reason the programme was funded, yet it is almost entirely absent from the arithmetic above**, because none of it bears on whether the catch can be made.

**Two of this article's instruments have limits.** The loop analysis reaches a result that depends on an architectural choice the record does not report, so the article computes both branches and claims neither, which is weaker than it would like to be. **And the survey behind the keystone is a conference literature rather than an agency-report one**, at 23.5 percent from one aeronautical society and 21.0 percent from one engineering institute against 13.4 percent from the two agency report servers combined, shares of the keystone cluster's records that The Definition of Primary counts. **A reader who expected the report literature to carry this subject would be disappointed, and the reason lies in where the work was published.**

## The Source Base

**The survey holds 5,700 research records, and every one of them is cited across 22 clusters.** They come from the Crossref registry, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's technical reports server and the Defense Technical Information Center's registry prefix. A further 125 references are not research records, being the primary documents, the reference works, the books and the back-references to earlier articles in this series.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's technical reports server, on the Defense Technical Information Center's own server or on the Office of Scientific and Technical Information's, or when it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. By that rule 886 records, 15.5 percent, are report primaries. **The rule does not reach the society and journal papers in which most of this subject was published**, so the share is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand.

**The keystone is less report-heavy than the survey around it.** **The keystone cluster is 23.5 percent papers from the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics and 21.0 percent from the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, against 13.4 percent from the agency report servers.** Each share counts the cluster's 119 records by the address each one cites, being the society's registry prefix 10.2514, the institute's prefix 10.1109, and for the agency reports the rule above.

**The reason is that this subject was published at conferences rather than in agency report series.** Of the 48 keystone records dated before 2009, 19 are papers of the aeronautical society, and of the 71 dated 2009 or later, 23 are papers of the engineering institute. **Only three records in the whole survey carry mid-air or aerial recovery in the title and are also agency reports.** A thin primary fraction here is a fact about where the work was published.

### Thin Subjects

**The keystone cluster is small, at 119 records, and seven of the 22 clusters are smaller still.** It is gathered in the field's own vocabulary as well as in this article's, including aerial recovery and the mothership, cable and drogue arrangement by name, so its size is not an artefact of phrasing.

**It is small for the third of three reasons a cluster can be thin.** A cluster can be thin because the heading is wrong, because the work is filed under another subject, or because the work was never done. **Here it is the third.** The specialist directory records the October 2021 recovery as the first time an X-61A was retrieved in mid-air, after several unsuccessful attempts \[[Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_dusrm_x61]\], and recovery of a flying uncrewed aircraft by a flying transport had little literature before it. What the cluster holds is mid-air retrieval of payloads descending under parachutes from the nineteen sixties onward, net, ship and ground recovery of small remotely piloted aircraft, and from 2009 a body of simulation work on the three-body recovery problem. **The programme's own technical account of the recovery is a conference paper of 2024** \[[Carter, Keeter and Calhoun][ref_scitech_2024]\], cited as a primary source and not counted among the research records.

**Six further subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group.

**Starting the engine at altitude is an old subject of crewed aircraft.** Of the 14 titles, 7 date from before 1960, and none names a turbofan, a small engine or an expendable one, so the cold start the vehicle had to make rests on the programme's own release rather than on a published analysis of an engine of its class.

**The Bode identity has no title literature in the survey**, so the statement that a loop cannot reject a disturbance at every frequency rests on the identity as Holding Station To Inches states it rather than on surveyed work.

**Turning a recovered vehicle round has four titles**, one on the regeneration of a reusable military launch vehicle between flights and the rest on airline turnaround, so the twenty-four hour claim stands on the programme's releases alone.

**The aerodynamic damping of a towed cable has two titles**, one on the damping section of a towed array and one on the damping of a vibrating stay cable, so the damping ratio this article derives rests on the linearised drag relation rather than on measurement.

**Arresting the tumble after release has one title, and it concerns docking with a tumbling spacecraft**, and an operator's reaction time has none, so both the rate capture and the human-loop budget rest on the primary record and on stated assumptions.

**Each conclusion is tested twice, once in the words this article uses and once in the words the field uses**, because a thin count under an article's own phrasing is a fact about the phrasing. ### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject**, meaning a subject the article's argument uses, being the capture and its antecedents, the towed body and cable, the wake, relative navigation and docking, release from the carrier, the vehicle and its comparators, parachutes, multi-vehicle operation, the engine, reuse and cost, flight control and gusts, flight test, and the aerodynamics, performance and atmosphere the sizing uses. Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded. Turnaround also names the maintenance turnaround of refineries, process plants and companies. A towed sonar array is often a subject in signal processing rather than in the dynamics of the towed body. Low cost, the learning curve and life-cycle costing are production-economics terms before they are aeronautical ones. The range equation of radar and laser ranging is not the Breguet one, Breguet is also a family of watchmakers, Discoverer is also the name of proteomics software, and parachute is also a word of cardiology, finance, music and children's play. Supervisory control also names a theory of discrete-event systems, AirDrop also names a file-sharing protocol, and pose estimation also names the estimation of human, hand and road-vehicle pose. Correction, erratum, retraction and withdrawal notices, news items, dictionary headwords and records for whole conference volumes are excluded as well, because a survey counts research works. A review of a book, a glossary of terms, a reference or definition entry of two pages or fewer and a second deposit of a document already in the survey are not admitted either, while an authored encyclopedia article of more than two pages and a textbook chapter are research works and are kept.

**Three of this subject's words are severe collisions.** Asked for a bare `gremlin`, the Crossref registry returns a bone morphogenetic protein antagonist, a children's therapy series, an Oxford English Dictionary headword, a 1943 note in `Notes and Queries` and a horror film. For a bare `gremlins` it returns a reconfigurable-robotics architecture and a statistical package for multipartite networks. **And `retrieval` is the worst of them**, because in atmospheric and Earth remote sensing retrieval is the word for inverting a measurement. **Docking is as hard**, because computational chemistry uses the word for fitting a molecule to a binding site, and the phrase `docking and molecular dynamics` satisfies any qualifier an aerospace subject would reach for. A docking record is therefore excluded when its title carries the vocabulary of drug discovery, rather than admitted when it carries an aerospace word.

**A broad term collides in the ordinary way.** A bare `unmanned aerial vehicle` brings in object detectors, drone photography, crop and forest survey, power line inspection, communication relays and drone light shows, and these are excluded as applications in domains the argument does not use. **The vehicles also exclude by kind.** Multirotor, tilt-rotor, ducted-fan and tail-sitter drones, helicopters and other powered-lift aircraft share the words but not the flight mechanics of a fixed-wing vehicle caught by a transport, so they are excluded except where the title is a recovery, towing, launch, formation, wake-encounter or refuelling subject. Supersonic aerodynamics, projectiles, airships, re-entry and the launch vehicles' own guidance are excluded for the same reason, and so are ship and orbital station keeping, which share a phrase and not a problem.

**Two neighbouring literatures are admitted deliberately, and the reasons are different.** **Missile literature is admitted** because the airframe is a cruise missile with wings and the engine is the one in the Tomahawk, so launch transients, carriage, separation and folding-wing deployment are this article's subject. **Marine towed-body literature is admitted as well.** A towed cable in water is the same differential equation in a denser fluid, the underwater literature is much the older and better documented half of it, and the aerodynamic towed-body literature alone would leave this article's keystone nearly empty. **The price is visible in the towed-body cluster**, which carries a great deal of work on underwater vehicles and ship towing, and the article says so rather than presenting the cluster as aeronautical.

**Defence acquisition policy is deliberately not held, and one conclusion rests on a primary document rather than on this survey because of it.** The article measures the programme's outcome against a schedule its own Request for Information stated in 2014, and the conclusions table under Thin Subjects finds no cited records under the field's words for schedule and cost growth in acquisition. Admitting the acquisition-policy literature would bring a very large body of work about defence procurement into an article about catching an aeroplane, and none of it would bear on whether the catch can be made. **The conclusion is carried by the document that states the plan and the record that shows the outcome. A survey that excludes a subject has not measured it.** The same holds for the payload, the operational concept and the autonomy architecture. **A survey that excludes a subject has not measured it**, and this article draws no conclusion about any of the three.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Vortex-induced vibration of circular cylinders and stay cables, the cable motion of towed sonar arrays and oceanographic towed bodies, spacecraft formation flying and docking, vision-based relative pose estimation, differential satellite positioning of vehicles not named as aircraft, and a few applications of learning curves and availability models to production in general each share either the physics of a towed cable and a docking or the economics of a reusable fleet with this subject, so each is kept and a reader may weigh it accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

### What the Record Establishes

**The register's description of the X-61A is not official Department of Defense wording**, and the compiler says so in a note above the table. The date, the designation, the contractor, the engine and the sponsor are official. The mission statement is not. **This is the first research designation for which that is true among the X rows the register dates in full**, measured across all 31 X rows.

**The programme ran from 2015 to 2021, from four teams to two to one**, with Phase 1 awarded 31 March 2016, Phase 2 on 15 March 2017 and Phase 3 to Dynetics in April 2018. Five air vehicles were built. **The agency's programme page now states that the programme is complete** \[[DARPA][ref_darpa_gremlins]\].

**Nine sorties were flown in four series for eighteen hours, two vehicles were lost, three remain.** The sorties in the four series sum exactly to the stated total, and the airframes built less those lost equal those remaining.

**One airborne recovery was achieved, on 29 October 2021, after at least nine previous attempts each of which came within inches.**

### What Is Computed Rather Than Reported

**The depth of maximum wake gradient behind a transport aeroplane is a fixed fraction of its wing span**, being the span times pi over eight root three, which for the C-130 is 30.1 feet. This is an identity and contains no assumption about weight, speed, density or altitude. **The formation station at 125 feet sits 4.16 times deeper than that, where the gradient is 6.19 times flatter.**

**A passively towed cable settles to an inclination fixed by its weight and its drag, and by nothing else.** At 200 knots at 10,000 feet a ten millimetre steel wire rope settles at 14.9 degrees. **A cable that would hang at forty-five degrees would have to weigh 10.4 times what that rope weighs.** The passive geometry therefore does not produce the arrangement the programme used, and so the docking device is attitude-controlled.

**The X-61A carries 1,922 newtons per metre of span against 3,909 for the cruise missile that shares its engine**, so its induced drag at a given dynamic pressure is smaller by a factor of 4.14. This uses published weights and published spans and no estimate.

**An uncontrolled vehicle leaves a six inch capture window in 0.99 seconds in a one metre per second gust**, and the position loop that holds it needs a bandwidth of about 0.228 hertz, 1.3 times the fundamental transverse mode of the cable the docking device hangs from.

**The relative kinetic energy at a 1960 Corona canopy snatch was about 165.1 kilojoules against a few hundred joules for a vehicle that has matched speed**, a factor of 486.

**A flyaway cap of 700,000 dollars and a 20-use life are one requirement**, and its value is 35,000 dollars of airframe per sortie.

**The towed cable is too heavily damped to ring**, at a modal damping ratio of 0.324 on its fundamental, which decays by a factor of e in 0.49 of a cycle. **No loop can reject a disturbance at every frequency, by an identity rather than a rule of thumb**, and the two standard forms of a second-order position loop differ in relative degree, so one must amplify somewhere and the other need not. The one that need not pays **140 times** more high-frequency noise for it.

**A design life saturates against attrition.** An airframe that can be lost with probability epsilon on any sortie delivers a geometric sum rather than its design life, and that sum cannot pass one over epsilon. **At five percent per sortie the ceiling is exactly twenty**, the required life, so the requirement is only specifiable below that rate.

**The polar allows a lift to drag ratio of at most 13.27** at the bounded aspect ratio, and the best-range Mach number at 35,000 feet is 0.59 against a published maximum of 0.6.

**The three contracts sum to 82,680,983.37 dollars across 38 modifications**, each total equalling the sum of its transactions to the cent. **The pandemic is priced at 5,852,178.74 dollars by modifications that name it**, amounting to 11.18 percent of the Phase 3 contract.

### What Is Assumed

**The recovery airspeed, altitude and aircraft weight are not published** and are taken as 200 knots, 10,000 feet and the mean of the C-130A's empty and maximum weights. The wake results scale with all three and the identity for the worst depth does not.

**The cable's diameter and linear density are not published** and three combinations are carried rather than one. The normal drag coefficient is taken as 1.2 and the tangential friction coefficient as 0.02, and the towed body is taken to weigh 50 kilograms and to have 200 newtons of drag.

**The wing area, the lift to drag ratio, the zero-lift drag coefficient and the specific fuel consumption are not published.** The wing area is bounded rather than estimated, and the other three are varied across a band.

**The capture window is inferred from the phrase within inches** and is carried at six and at twelve inches.

**The turbulence is represented both ways.** A sharp-edged gust gives the acceleration the drift time is computed from, and the von Karman spectrum gives the share of the disturbance energy that falls inside the loop's band, 89.4 percent of it. **The two agree**, in the sense that almost all of the energy is where the crude model implicitly put it, and the scale length and intensity of the spectrum are assumed.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**The engine.** The official record names an F107-WR-105 and the only published rating for that dash number is twice what the public descriptions of the vehicle state. **This article does not resolve it** and reports both.

**The designation date.** The register gives 6 June 2019 and the prime contractor's subcontractor gives August 2019.

**The turnaround.** The agency writes twenty-four working hours and the contractor writes approximately twenty-four hours, about the same event.

**The number of docking attempts in the fourth series**, so the success rate above is a bound rather than a figure.

**Which control architecture the vehicle used.** A second-order position loop can put its damping term in the forward path or in a minor loop, and the two give opposite answers about whether the loop amplifies the docking device's motion. **The article computes both and claims neither.**

**What a recovery sortie costs**, the term that dominates the cost identity once only one vehicle comes home per sortie.

**Why the programme stopped.** The agency's page says the programme is complete \[[DARPA][ref_darpa_gremlins]\] and its 2021 release says the team would determine next steps \[[DARPA][ref_darpa_recovery]\]. **No cancellation, transition or follow-on decision has been found and none is claimed.**

## Out of Scope

**The payloads and the operational concept.** What the vehicles would have carried and how a volley would have been employed are the reason the programme existed and bear on none of the arithmetic here.

**The autonomy stack.** The vehicle is described as semi-autonomous with one operator controlling up to four \[[Leidos][ref_leidos_captured]\] or up to eight \[[Dynetics X-61 Gremlins][ref_x61_wikipedia]\] depending on the source, and the architecture of that autonomy is not examined.

**The wider attritable-aircraft programmes.** The [XQ-58][related_post_a355_x58_slot_taken_by_xq58] and its relatives \[[Kratos XQ-58 Valkyrie][ref_xq58]\] share a procurement philosophy with this vehicle and not its problem.

**Underwater towed bodies**, whose literature this article deliberately admits because the equations are the same, are not treated as a subject in their own right.

**Any assessment of whether the capability should have been pursued**, which is a question about policy and not about whether the catch can be made.

## Conclusion

**The register stops being a primary source at this designation and the evidence changes kind because of it.** For the [X-60A][related_post_a357_generation_orbit_x60] the government's own sentence about the vehicle could be read closely enough to carry a whole argument. For the X-61A there is no such sentence. The official record is a date, a designation, a contractor, an engine and a sponsor, and everything else in the register's row is a compiler's reconstruction, marked as one. **Of the 31 X rows the register carries, and among those it dates in full, the X-60A is the last whose description is official wording and the X-61A is the first whose description is not.** The register only covers allocations made after 19 August 1998 \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\], so most of this series has no row to read at all. **What is new here is a row that exists and declines to say what the aeroplane was for.**

**What it did say, in one of the cells that are official, is an engine that disagrees with the public accounts by a factor of two.** The F107-WR-105 is documented at 1,400 pounds of thrust and the vehicle is publicly described with 700. Neither figure changes the conclusions here, because at Mach 0.6 both are several times the drag, and **the published maximum speed is therefore a choice rather than a ceiling on either reading**.

**The vehicle is not a cruise missile and its published dimensions prove it without a single estimate.** It carries 1,922 newtons per metre of span where the cruise missile sharing its engine carries 3,909, so its induced drag at a given dynamic pressure is 4.14 times smaller. **A vehicle that has to come home and fly formation with a transport has to be efficient at the transport's speed, and of the two levers that buy that, span is the one that does not cost payload.**

**The hard part is the last few metres, and the arithmetic shows why.** The worst place to hold station behind a transport is a fixed fraction of its span, 30.1 feet for a C-130, and the programme's formation station sits 4.16 times deeper where the gradient is 6.19 times flatter. A passively towed cable hangs at an angle set by its weight and drag and cannot be told where to go, so the docking device has to fly. **And the position loop that must hold a vehicle inside a six inch window needs about 0.228 hertz, while the cable that device hangs from responds at 0.176. The loop's crossover sits between the first and second modes of its target.** That cable is too heavily damped to ring, at a damping ratio of 0.324 on its fundamental, **and the damping removes the ringing without moving the tracking problem**, because a loop cannot reject motion at a frequency it crosses over on whatever produces the motion.

**The C-130 had been catching things in mid-air since 1961 and the difference is that this one was flying.** A Corona canopy snatch engaged at about 165.1 kilojoules of relative energy and needed a winch that could absorb it. A vehicle that has matched speed engages at a few hundred joules and needs nothing of the structure. **The difficulty did not go away. It moved from the hardware into the guidance**, and nine attempts within inches is what that move cost.

**The programme answered the feasibility question and could not begin on the reliability one.** Four vehicles recovered in under thirty minutes was the objective and one vehicle recovered was the result, in a mission that was not attempting the rate. A twenty-use life was the requirement and the fleet flew 45 percent of the sorties that one life test needs. **The economics survive that easily, because even five uses brings the airframe cost per sortie to 140,000 dollars, so twenty was never the break-even.** **And what twenty provides turns out to saturate.** An airframe that can be lost on any sortie delivers the sum of a geometric series rather than its design life, and that sum cannot pass the reciprocal of the loss rate however long the life is. At five percent per sortie the ceiling is exactly twenty, so the requirement is only specifiable if the loss rate is well below it. **The reliability question and the economics question are the same relation asked twice**, which neither half of this article could see alone.

**The record's last word is not in the publicity at all.** The agency's page calls the programme complete \[[DARPA][ref_darpa_gremlins]\]. Its release of November 2021 records that the team would analyse the data and determine next steps \[[DARPA][ref_darpa_recovery]\]. **No decision is recorded either way in the programme publications cited here.**

**The contract tells more than the publicity does.** The last positive obligation is 47 days after the recovery, and the period of performance then ran on for 1,463 days carrying nothing but zero-dollar modifications. **A programme that stops paying and stays open has decided something.** The [X-60A][related_post_a357_generation_orbit_x60] did the reverse, obligating 30.1 percent of its money after it stopped being visible, and ending by paying to ship equipment.

**Two articles, two programmes, and the same lesson from opposite directions.** The publicity is not the record. **Here it is the money that stops speaking first**, and there it was the money that went on speaking after everything else had stopped.
